videos.full_text: Hi, my name is Julie Klinney and I am a computer science PhD student at Stanford University and I'm excited to be talking about our paper, Mission Impossible Language Models. I want to give a big thank you to my wonderful co-authors. Just a few months ago, there was a short correspondence in nature that made three big claims about why AI doesn't model human language. I could talk at length about each of the claims the authors bring up, but I'm going to focus on this third one. Here, the authors state that large language models can produce impossible languages, or those not generated by the principles governing all known human languages, just as well as, if not better than, natural language output and cannot distinguish between them. Similar claims have been made by several linguists including Nome Chomsky and his New York Times article from last year. For these authors, LLMs learn possible and impossible languages equally well, and so it follows that LLMs do not model the structure of human language and cannot tell us anything about language. This claim, if true, would have significant consequences for linguistic methodology, and potentially also for the viability of LLMs as the basis for robust language capabilities. What we set out to do is actually put this claim to the test. We trained some language models on impossible languages and tried to observe whether they are learned just as well as the possible languages. But first, you might be wondering, what exactly is a possible or impossible human language? Well, this question lacks a very clear answer. If we take the characterization of language as it is presented in much of theoretical linguistics, then all human languages are thought to have hierarchical structures, syntactic structures generated through recursive rules. And we could represent these sentences through these hierarchical syntax trees. So if we granted the possible languages are defined by these hierarchical structures, what are the impossible languages? Well, these would be languages that have the opposite type of rules or rules that are not hierarchically structured. More concretely, these rules are based on the linear order of words or rigidly determined by word positions. So if we take the same syntax tree I showed before, we can make an impossible language by introducing a rule that violates the hierarchical structure. As an example, we can look at how tense is marked in this sentence. It is marked by an s suffix on the verb. What if the way English marked verb inflection was by placing the tense marker a fixed number of words later? This would be a completely systematic pattern, but no language uses counting and inserting markers in this way to signify verb inflection. It's a completely unnatural pattern. What I just showed you was an example of a language that involves linear counting rules. But I think that this is a narrow account of what is impossible. In our paper, we test on a much wider range of impossible languages and place them on a scale we call the impossibility continuum. We know that the real languages in the world are possible for humans to learn by definition, and they are hierarchically structured. The languages involving count-based grammar rules like the one I've shown are close to the attested languages, but they include rules that do not conform to the hierarchical structure of attested languages. Beyond these languages, we also test languages of reverse strings and languages with shuffled word orders. And in constructing these impossible languages, we consider both their information theoretic attributes relevant to machine learning, as well as their formal linguistic characteristics. And we signify the boundary between possible and impossible with a question mark to indicate that these distinctions are currently fuzzy. Our methodology could be used to explore this boundary for LLMs. So how do we test whether language models reflect this impossibility continuum? In our experiments, we create synthetic impossible language data sets by altering English data. For the base corpus, we use the 100 million word BVLM data set. And then we train a GPT-2 small model from scratch for each synthetic data set. These models are not retrained, and they've only seen data in the impossible language. Then we use test set perplexities as a general metric for the extent to which a model has learned an impossible language. In the paper, we group the languages into three classes based in the continuum I had shown previously, and we call these the shuffle, reverse, and hop languages, where the hop languages are the count-based languages I motivated earlier. And these are the perplexity plots across model training steps for all of the impossible languages. I won't be able to go into each of the languages here, but I want to draw your attention to the bottom lines on each of these graphs. These are the control languages that represent unaltered English, and in all cases the natural control language had lower perplexities than all of the impossible languages. While there are clear distinctions for the shuffle and reverse classes, the distinctions among the hop languages are pretty subtle, so we will be taking a closer look at these languages with a more targeted evaluation. I want to first detail how the hop languages are constructed. First, no hop is the control language, which represents English, but there are a few preprocessing steps we take to make this inadequate control. First, we limitize all third-person present tense verbs, so in this sentence the verb, cleans, is changed to clean. Then we insert a marker representing the verb's tense and number right next to the verb. This isolates verb tense and number into a single marker. Then finally, we tokenize the sentence. In these examples, differently colored blocks represent different GPT-2 tokens, and the verb marker is represented by its own token. Next, we have the token hop language. Here we pre-process the sentence in the same way, but this time we insert the marker exactly for tokens after the verb. Finally, in the word hop language, we do the same thing, but this time we insert the marker token four words after the verb, so you can see that this time the marker respects word boundaries. So how can we better test whether GPT-2 prefers the more natural control? We next devise an experiment that uses surprises to measure how well each of the hot models can predict the placement of its verb marker tokens. What we want to know from this experiment is first, whether each hot model learns to expect verb marker tokens at the correct locations, and second, how surprised is the model when verb marker tokens do not appear when they're supposed to? And what we do is create these pairs of grammatical and ungrammatical sentences in which the verb marker token appears and does not appear. And then we can get the surprise of the verb marker token in the grammatical construction and the surprise of the token after it in the ungrammatical construction. If the hot model has learned its respective verb marking rule, then the surprise of the verb marker in the grammatical constructions should be small. And the surprise of the verb marker and the token that follows it should be large. We take a sample of test sentences and measure the means marker surprises and the mean surprise of differences for each of the hot models over training steps. So again, these are the three hot languages for reference, and here are the results for the first surprise experiment. The left bar in each graph is the control model and you can see that it has the smallest marker surprises across all intervals of training steps. Both of the impossible languages have higher marker surprises, but interestingly, the token hot model does better than the word hot model, indicating the GPT-2 is better at learning the counting rule when the unit being counted is a token. And this result is also supported by the surprise of different symmetric. The control has the largest surprise of difference across training steps, followed by the token hot model. So based on the results of these surprise experiments, GPT-2 favors the natural grammar rule, but it is also capable of acquiring a count based grammar rule. I won't have time to go into it here, but our paper includes a deep dive into the internal mechanisms of the hot models using causal abstraction analysis. So you can check that out if you're interested. With these results in mind, I want to return to the motivation I had at the beginning of the talk and ask, do LLMs learn possible and impossible languages equally well? In this work, we show that GPT-2 can distinguish between possible and impossible languages, challenging previous unfounded assertions about LLMs. And more importantly, this work shows that LLMs can tell us a lot about language, complementing and defending a rich line of work showing that LLMs can learn syntactic or more general linguistic principles just from data. Since we found that GPT-2 had an easier time learning the possible languages, this leads to the question about what inductive bias does GPT-2 have that matches natural language? We make the argument that it has to do with information locality or the property that, when parts of text predict each other, they are often close together. And a preference for locality arises in GPT-2 due to the incremental nature of its causal language modeling objective. We see this work as a call to action for research and architectures with different inductive biases that may be even better than GPT at finding the possible versus impossible distinction. To conclude, our paper opens up a new question about how LLMs can help us identify possible learn possible languages and bring us closer to defining the boundary between these two classes of languages. And we've made the case that LLMs are clearly relevant to investigations and claims about language learning and can be used as a tool for exploring questions like what can be learned from data or what sorts of innate priors are necessary for language learning. Arguments that by design, they are unlimited in what they can learn or incapable of distinguishing the possible from the impossible do not offer convincing evidence otherwise. Thank you.

videos.full_text: Hi everyone, my name is Anubhav. In this presentation, I am going to talk about NERMQMRC, which is named into recognition using multi-question machine reading comprehension. The presentation is outlined as follows. We are going to talk about what is name netted recognition, how it was traditionally solved using sequence labeling task, how NER is now being solved using machine reading comprehension as a single question answering task, and then our proposed solution of multi-question machine reading comprehension. Coming to what is name netted recognition, NERMQMRC is basically a task to classify and locate name entities in an unstructured text. As you can see in this example, we have this unstructured text where we are able to identify mens as department, red as color, cantabil as ran, and solid as the pattern type. NERMQMRC is used in multiple places in the industry such as identifying product attributes from product text, identifying the attributes from search queries, and also identifying slot values from customer conversations with Alexa. Traditionally, NERMQMRC has been posed as a sequence labeling task using biolus-tm architecture. The unstructured text goes in the input for the model and outcomes the bio-label encoding for each of the relevant tokens. In this architecture, if there are K entities, we would require 2k plus 1 label. The proofs for the sequence labeling task are that it can classify multiple entities in a single forward pass, which is why there is faster training and inference due to a single forward pass for all entities. The cons include the label space increases with the number of increase in the entities. The entity information is not included in the text rather, it is just present in the classification layer, and if there are new labels to be added, it needs to retrain the complete model again. In recent literature, NERMQMRC has also been solved using machine reading comprehension. Machine reading comprehension is a task to read and comprehend a given text and then answer a question based on it. When we pose NERMQMRC as a machine reading comprehension, each entity is asked as a question for the context, and the answer is the span of the entity in the unstructured text. This approach uses pre-trained word-transform based architecture to extract the span of the question from the context. Entity value is obtained using the start and end for bio-label. The proofs of NERMQMRC approach is that the entity information is present in the input of the model itself. The output label space remains constant as there are only two labels for start end or three labels for bio-label encoding for any kind of entities, and it can also give answers for unseen entities because of the large pre-trained word model and no increase in the label space. The con for this approach is that multiple entities cannot be extracted in a single forward pass because each question is just one single entity. This leads to slow training and inference due to multiple processes for extracting all the entities, which brings us to our proposed solution NERMQMRC which is best of both worlds. It is able to scale up for entities very well. It is also able to score for multiple entities in a single forward pass. The training time and the inference time improves substantially because of this and the entity information is present within the model input as well. Our proposed solution NERMQMRC asks questions around all the entities in a single forward pass. As you can see the difference for SQMRC, each entity is asked a separate question whereas for MQMRC all the entities related to the same context are asked within a single forward pass. Each entity is separated by a special token which we add to the word vocabulary called ENT. Each ENT token is responsible for holding the information for the adjacent entity. The ENT embedding for each attribute is then used to produce the entity specific context embeddings by performing the element-wise multiplication of ENT embedding and the context embeddings. The entity specific context embedding is then passed on to a linear classifier to produce the span and cell for each of the entities. To create the input for our architecture, we group the entities which belong to the same product. We also explicitly add entities which are not present in the text to promote the model to learn when an entity is not present. Using this data creation process we are able to substantially reduce the overall volume of the training data set. The plot on the right shows the number of entities which belong to the same product in their respective data sets. Coming to the results of the model, first talking about the model runtime MQMRC on an average has 2.5 times faster training and 2.3 times faster inference as compared to SQMRC approach. Talking about the NER task performance of MQMRC with respect to various baselines for all the benchmark data sets, MQMRC is able to outperform SQMRC. It is also able to reduce the number of models for NERSL by training a single model instead of five different ensemble models in the e-commerce 5PT data set. Coming to the few shot experiments, we observe that MQMRC is also able to scale well even when having less number of training samples. As you can see from the plot, even when using the complete data set the NERSL approach was only able to reach 74.29% F1 score whereas MQMRC was able to perform better than the baseline even with as low as 2.5K during training. We also experimented with different context and entity embedding interaction operations. We tried operations such as doing some of the entity embedding with the token embedding or taking the difference, the product and applying activation functions to it as well as taking the max. The result suggests that having entity operations which creates a large disparity between the different elements of a token embedding helps us to get the better embedding space. We also experimented with the entity ordering in a question. Keeping the entity ordering same in the question during training leads to deterioration of F1 by 12.3% when we shuffle the entity questions during inference. This is likely due to the model giving more weightage to the position while learning the entry representations and not focusing on the entity name. Shuffling the order of entities during training alleviates this issue. MQMRC has multiple benefits when implemented in production systems. It reduces the model training and inference caused by an average of 58.82 percent in our experiments. It has faster model run times as compared to the NERSL approach. It reduces the model proliferation and maintenance of multiple models by training a single model for large number of entities and it is able to perform better than both NERSQMRC and NER SLB approaches. So to conclude, we proposed posing NER as a multi-question machine reading comprehension task because it is much more faster during training and inference and also is cost effective in production systems and scalable for large number of entities while maintaining the performance. Thank you.
